question: What is the estimated cost of reconstruction needs for Ukraine's energy infrastructure? (Ước tính thiệt hại tái thiết cơ sở hạ tầng năng lượng Ukraine là bao nhiêu?)

gold.evidence:
Attacks to Ukraine’s energy infrastructure have created an estimated $91 billion 
in reconstruction needs.

results.text:
In March, the World Bank released the updated Rapid Damage and Needs 
Assessment for Ukraine, which emphasized the need for both public and private 
funds to address an estimated $411 billion in reconstruction and recovery costs over 
the next 10 years. The highest estimated needs are in transport, housing, energy, 
social protection and livelihoods, explosive-hazard management, and agriculture.

Attacks to Ukraine’s energy infrastructure have created an estimated $91 billion 
in reconstruction needs. The World Bank Group is supporting the Government of 
Ukraine to develop a European Union (EU)-aligned energy sector strategy to restore 
security of supply, reestablish financial viability, mobilize private capital at scale, 
strengthen corporate governance of state energy companies, and improve financial 
sustainability — essential ingredients for economic competitiveness, productivity, and 
employment creation.

For its part, MIGA has extended and increased 
guarantees to free up capital linked to two banks’ mandatory reserves, issuing 
$448 million in new guarantees since February 2022 to keep small businesses

question: What proportion of Cabo Verde's GDP does the tourism sector account for? (Ngành du lịch đóng góp bao nhiêu phần trong GDP của Cabo Verde?)

gold.evidence:
Tourism is an engine of Cabo Verde’s economy, accounting for over a 
quarter of GDP.

results.text:
The results are reshaping Cabo Verde’s tourism landscape. Average daily 
tourist spending and overnight stays in previously under-visited islands 
are both rising, and growing private investment signals confidence in the 
country’s trajectory. With the World Bank Group supporting the full arc from 
governance and infrastructure to skills and private finance, Cabo Verde is 
building a more diversified, sustainable, and job-rich tourism economy.

Tourism is an engine of Cabo Verde’s economy, accounting for over a 
quarter of GDP. But for years, the sector has been constrained by a narrow 
model dominated by all-inclusive resorts in only two of the archipelago’s 
10 islands, with few links to local businesses. Infrastructure deficits, a 
shortage of skilled hospitality workers, and the absence of a coherent 
framework for attracting quality investment left the country exposed and 
its potential unrealized.

results.text:
Water security is foundational for productivity and economic growth. As one 
of the most water-scarce countries in the world, Jordan has struggled to grow 
its economy and create jobs for its young people. The government of Jordan is taking bold action to boost water security by 
initiating its largest-ever infrastructure project, the Aqaba-Amman Water 
Desalination and Conveyance Project. By 2030, the project is expected 
to deliver approximately 40 percent of Jordan’s domestic water supply.

Complementing the Aqaba-Amman project is IBRD’s $300 million Jordan 
Water Sector Efficiency Project, which includes financing from partners. This 
is strengthening Jordan’s broader water sector through non-revenue water 
reduction, energy efficiency, and distribution-system readiness. The World Bank Group’s support for Jordan’s water sector aligns with our 
Water Strategy Implementation Plan, which outlines how investments, 
long-term policy reforms, and institutional sustainability can deliver water 
security, economic growth, and job creation.

question: What health crisis causes high rates of premature death and disability in Pacific Island countries? (Khủng hoảng y tế nào gây tử vong sớm ở các quốc đảo Thái Bình Dương?)

gold.evidence:
Pacific Island countries face some of the world’s highest rates of premature death and 
disability from non-communicable disease, including diabetes,

results.text:
Pacific Island countries face some of the world’s highest rates of premature death and 
disability from non-communicable disease, including diabetes, cardiovascular disease, 
and cancer, alongside persistent communicable diseases. Local healthcare systems 
struggle to provide care to dispersed populations, and the resulting inefficiencies drive 
up service costs and hamper job creation and long-term growth. The World Bank’s Pacific Healthy Islands Transformation (PHIT) project, approved in 
fiscal 2026, is taking a new approach to improving the health of people across the 
region.

In the Philippines, we are working 
to address the persistence of high levels of childhood undernutrition and reverse the 
trends that could seriously damage the country’s human and economic potential. In Timor-Leste, we are helping the government better prepare for, prevent, respond 
to, and mitigate the impact of epidemics; while in T uvalu, we are supporting efforts 
to improve health service delivery, strengthen health management systems, and 
respond promptly and effectively to crises or emergencies.

health systems that can better prevent, prepare for, and respond to future shocks 
while maintaining essential health services. Our Change Cannot Wait report pres-
ents how countries can improve health outcomes by anticipating and adapting to 
health dynamics such as aging, stunting, non-communicable diseases, inequalities, 
and climate-related illnesses. We work with countries to screen for climate-related 
health risks—including food insecurity and poor diets, which affect vulnerable peo-
ple in particular—and identify effective ways to tackle them.

question: By what percentage can low-carbon development strategies reduce emissions without harming growth? (Chiến lược phát thải carbon thấp có thể giảm bao nhiêu % khí thải mà không hại tăng trưởng?)

gold.evidence:
Collectively, the low-carbon development strategies from these reports can reduce 
emissions by 70 percent, without harming growth.

results.text:
Covering over 20 countries, the first set of these reports show that climate change 
poses a major threat to long-term development objectives, but countries can grow 
while reducing emissions if they embrace major change. The financing to drive the 
transition averages about 1.4 percent of GDP , a manageable amount with appro-
priate private sector involvement. But in lower-income countries, financing needs 
can exceed 5 percent, which will require more support, including more conces -
sional resources, from high-income countries.

change, which can exacerbate risks and compound inequalities. Our Thriving report 
found that while cities in high- and upper-middle-income countries contribute sig-
nificantly to global CO2 emissions, cities in lower-income countries suffer the most 
from climate-related shocks and stresses due to poor management of urbanization 
pressures. This leads to sprawl, homes and businesses built in risky areas, traffic 
congestion, and more emissions.

Even though climate change is already exacting a heavy toll on the Philippines, 
the country has many of the tools required to reduce damages substantially, accord-
ing to the report for the country . And in Vietnam, the report suggested that with 
the right mix of policies and strategies, decarbonization efforts could help ensure 
that the country can meet growth and development goals while achieving net zero 
emissions. Building resilience and sustainability

question: What role does the World Bank serve regarding Financial Intermediary Funds (FIFs)? (Ngân hàng Thế giới đóng vai trò gì đối với các Quỹ FIFs?)

gold.evidence:
Financial intermediary funds (FIFs) represent large, 
distinct, multi-partner financing arrangements, for 
which the World Bank provides administrative support.

results.text:
FINANCIAL INTERMEDIARY FUNDS 
Financial intermediary funds (FIFs) represent large, 
distinct, multi-partner financing arrangements, for 
which the World Bank provides administrative support. They enable the international community to pool 
and coordinate funding from many sources to tackle 
specific development challenges, such as disease, 
food security, and other systemic changes. FIFs are 
independently governed, and the World Bank Group 
has no decision-making authority.

Instead, FIFs rely on 
the World Bank to provide financial and other services 
to facilitate their funding efforts and decisions. The 
World Bank serves as trustee for 27 FIFs. At the end of 
fiscal 2026, $45.2 billion was held in trust in the form 
of cash, investments, and promissory notes for FIFs. Seventeen FIFs have also selected the World Bank to 
host their secretariats, and 19 FIFs use World Bank 
Group institutions as their implementing entities. For more information, visit https://www. worldbank.org/en/about/unit/pim.

80 THE WORLD BANK ANNUAL REPORT 2023
Supporting countries through trust funds and financial 
intermediary funds
Through trust funds and financial intermediary funds, the Bank Group can deploy 
financing quickly, expand operations, and generate knowledge to help countries 
reduce poverty and boost shared prosperity in a sustainable way. These funds have 
provided financing, analytical support, and policy advice to respond to develop -
ment challenges such as COVID-19, climate change, the food and energy crises, and 
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

question: According to the 2023 report, how does gender equality impact development in Western and Central Africa? (Bình đẳng giới tác động thế nào tới phát triển ở Tây và Trung Phi năm 2023?)

gold.evidence:
Gender equality is not only essential for building more inclusive societies, but it 
can also accelerate progress in other areas of development, from improving human 
capital and food security to addressing climate change

results.text:
THE RE GIONS 23
Empowering women and girls in Western and 
Central Africa
Gender equality is not only essential for building more inclusive societies, but it 
can also accelerate progress in other areas of development, from improving human 
capital and food security to addressing climate change and fragility. But despite 
progress, women and girls in Western and Central Africa have a 58 percent chance 
of not being enrolled in secondary school and a 20 percent chance of bearing chil-
dren as a teenager. Regardless of the sector in which they work, they can expect to 
earn less than men.

But across the continent, the program is attract -
ing more and more female students for whom “science has no gender. ” Currently, 
about 35 percent of students enrolled in the program across Africa are women. Our work with countries to advance gender equality is showing strong results. According to the World Bank’s most recent Women, Business, and the Law report, 
Gabon and Côte d’Ivoire were among the top reformers in Sub-Saharan Africa, 
increasing their index scores from 82.5 to 95 and from 83.1 to 95, respectively.

They are helping close gaps in earnings and 
economic opportunity, reduce gender-based violence, and afford women and girls’ 
voice and agency. Guided by our regional gender action plan for Western and Central 
Africa, the Bank will continue to work with countries across the region to drive trans-
formational change on the scale that women and girls deserve in order to ensure all 
people are able to achieve their full potential. Spotlight
